newsitem.title: USA: Clinton under pressure to name new CIA director.
newsitem.headline: Clinton under pressure to name new CIA director.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton is expected to act swiftly to designate a new CIA director after Monday's sudden withdrawal of his first nominee for the post, former national security adviser Anthony Lake.

Lake gave up the fight after three days of tough confirmation hearings last week, in which the Senate Intelligence Committee questioned his integrity, management skills and fitness to head U.S. intelligence operations.

One of Clinton's top advisers and an architect of U.S. policy on Bosnia, Haiti and Russia, Lake cited frustration over Republican efforts to turn his hearings into a "political football in a game with constantly moving goal posts."

Monday's developments surprised many who had predicted Lake's eventual confirmation and said he handled himself well during last week's often testy Senate hearings. The panel was due to resume hearings on Lake's nomination on Tuesday.

Lake's decision also marked a setback for Clinton, who counted Lake among his closest advisers and publicly went to bat for the nominee -- one of the final members of Clinton's second-term team awaiting Senate confirmation.
Lake met with Clinton at the White House on Monday to explain his decision, but had a hard time convincing the president to agree to withdraw his name, administration sources said.

"He met with the president today and the president very reluctantly, and after trying to convince Tony to fight it, accepted his personal judgment that he ought to withdraw his nomination," said one source, who asked not to be identified.
The source noted Lake first proposed withdrawing his name before last week's hearings, but was dissuaded at that point.
One administration source said Lake had become convinced the committee would "nibble him to death rather than deal with the nomination straight-up anytime soon."

Lake's nomination was dogged by questions about why his staff did not inform him of an FBI briefing on an alleged Chinese plan to influence U.S. elections, and his decision to keep Congrss in the dark about tacit U.S. approval of Iranian arms shipments to Bosnian Moslems in 1994.

He was expected to face more grilling about a report that surfaced Monday alleging that a controversial oil man visited Clinton at the White House despite objections by Lake's National Security Council.
In a letter explaining his withdrawal, Lake called the confirmation process "nasty and brutish without being short," and said that "Washington has gone haywire" in partisanship.
No official confirmation was immediately available from the White House.

Senate Intelligence Committee Chairman Richard Shelby, an Alabama Republican, issued a statement late on Monday saying, "This nomination has been wrought with controversy from the beginning. Although I found Mr. Lake to be intelligent and amicable, I continue to have strong reservations about his fitness to be the director of central intelligence."
The ranking Democrat on the panel, Nebraska Sen. Bob Kerrey, said he regretted the circumstances surrounding Lake's withdrawal and called Lake's treatment by the panel "unfair."
Kerrey urged the panel to "put partisanship behind it" and act quickly to confirm Clinton's next nominee.
Former Clinton adviser George Stephanopoulos told ABC's "Nightline" he expected swift action on a new CIA nominee.

In his letter, Lake said he decided to quit because, "the longer this goes, the worse the damage," adding his hope that "sooner rather than later, people of all political views ... will demand that Washington give priority to policy over partisanship, to governing over 'gotcha.'"

Names circulating for the post include some who already hold a confirmed position, including Acting CIA Director George Tenet, who was once staff director for the Senate intelligence committee, and Deputy Attorney General Jamie Gorelick, who was up for the job before Lake was chosen.
